articles.summary: Thermokarst ponds, or trough ponds, typically form when the ice in permafrost melts. They can also drain quickly. Anna Liljedahl Florida gets a lot of attention for its sinkholes , especially when they swallow cars and entire houses. But its sinkhole risk has nothing on Alaska’s. Much of Alaska’s soil is permafrost – ground that remains below 32 degrees Fahrenheit (0 degrees Celsius) for at least two consecutive years. It is often rich with ice, but when that ice melts, the ground can collapse. As temperatures rise, that’s happening more often across the Arctic. The drug, daraxonrasib, which will be sold under the brand name Rasonque, is approved for metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma, the most common form of pancreatic cancer. Developed by Revolution Medicines, Rasonque is a once-daily pill designed to block RAS proteins that play a key role in driving tumor growth. The FDA approved Rasonque for adults with metastatic pancreatic cancer who have already received at least one cancer treatment, such as chemotherapy, or who cannot undergo combination treatment. articles.summary: On Wednesday, Meta, the company that owns Facebook and Instagram, announced a landmark legal settlement in a trial spanning 48 states, Washington, D.C., and three U.S. territories. In addition to paying up to $18 billion to those states and territories, the company has agreed to make significant changes to its social-media platforms, including imposing two-hour time limits for teens, stopping notifications during the school day, removing “like” counts and cosmetic filters, and limiting teen usage between midnight and 6 a.m. This is good news for children, and for their mental health. But today’s settlement marks the beginning, not the end, of long-sought changes from companies like Meta. For more than a decade, activists, parents, whistleblowers, and lawmakers have been fighting for regulations on the ability of social-media platforms to prey on the vulnerabilities of children’s underdeveloped brains. articles.summary: It is not every day that a company can settle a case for over $17 billion and celebrate. However, Meta’s proposed settlement of claims brought by a coalition originally led by 29 states on Wednesday is a remarkably good deal for a company facing potential penalties that Meta estimated could reach $1.4 trillion and years of litigation. In the end, the company may not even take a loss from the litigation. The proposed settlement ends the states’ federal case (but not the wider wave of litigation), following similar settlements in tobacco, opiates and other products. It will require Meta to make changes to its platform, though the company has already appeared to be moving to make such changes. The maximum payment of closer to $17.1 billion is tied to whether other social media companies, TikTok and YouTube, for example, adopt parallel protections for children. Clinicians use it to diagnose patients and scientists use it to guide research. Despite its wide impact, the DSM has never integrated biology in its diagnoses of mental illness. This omission was largely because the underlying biology of mental illness was too preliminary to be included in such a widely used clinical manual. stories.summary: The Trump administration is weighing which Canadian imports it might prohibit if Canadian officials retaliate further against US tariffs, a US official told Semafor. Canada announced earlier this week it would match the Trump administration’s latest levies, fueling fears of an escalating trade war between the two longtime allies after negotiations imploded last week. If Canada goes further, the US official said, its actions would provide the legal basis for the US to impose another round of tariffs on Canada under Section 338. The same legal authority could be used to prohibit imports from Canada, the US official added, and the Trump administration is analyzing those imports to determine which prohibitions would not disrupt US supply chains. President Donald Trump has already pledged to hike tariffs on Canadian steel as well as trucks, cars, and car parts to 50%, beginning Jan. 1.

articles.summary: The San Francisco Department of Police Accountability found that two officers used unnecessary force and violated department policies while arresting Matthew Ludwig in 2024 after an officer entered the wrong license plate number into a police database, leading them to mistakenly believe Ludwig was driving a stolen car. Body camera video showed the officers breaking Ludwig's car window, pulling him from the vehicle, and throwing him to the ground. They then pepper-sprayed him from inches away, even though the required minimum distance for pepper spray is more than four feet. The officers eventually discovered their mistake but still recommended that Ludwig be charged with resisting arrest. They also impounded his vehicle and later auctioned it off when he could not afford the fines to recover it. The department's findings were sent to the San Francisco Police Commission, which may discipline the officers. Ludwig, meanwhile, died in 2025.
